qs.q: A 28-year-old patient presents with severe sensitivity to cold in a recently restored maxillary first premolar. Clinical examination reveals no recurrent caries or marginal leakage. The most likely explanation for this persistent sensitivity involves a specific characteristic of dentin.
o: Increased permeability of the enamel-dentin junction.
Elevated osmotic pressure within the dentinal tubules.
Reduced calcification of peritubular dentin matrix.
Direct neural stimulation of odontoblastic processes.
Hydrodynamic fluid movement within the dentinal tubules.
qs.e: Cold stimuli cause rapid fluid movement in dentinal tubules, activating mechanoreceptors in the pulp, leading to sensitivity.

qs.q: A patient with Sjögren's syndrome experiences severe xerostomia. This condition primarily affects the exocrine function of salivary glands, leading to a significant reduction in saliva production. Which specific component of saliva's protective function against dental caries would be most compromised?
o: The enzymatic degradation of dietary carbohydrates.
The maintenance of oral mucosal tissue hydration.
The lubrication of oral tissues during mastication.
The initiation of protein digestion in the mouth.
The mechanical cleansing and dilution of acids.
qs.e: Reduced salivary flow compromises mechanical cleansing and dilution of acids, increasing caries risk.

qs.q: A first-year dental student needs to locate reliable peer-reviewed biomedical literature to support an assignment on dental caries. Which specific database is highlighted in the curriculum as the backbone of evidence-based practice for this purpose?
o: Medline via PubMed
Microsoft Excel
Google Web Directory

qs.q: Which of the following organisms is closely associated with dental caries?
o: Streptococcus mutans
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Streptococcus agalactiae
Neisseria subflava
qs.e: Streptococcus mutans is the main cause of dental caries.

qs.q: Which microorganism is closely associated with dental caries?
o: Neisseria subflava.
Streptococcus mutans.
Candida albicans.
Prevotella melaninogenica.
Staphylococcus epidermidis.
qs.e: S. mutans is the primary causative agent of dental caries. It produces acids from sugar metabolism that demineralize tooth enamel and produces sticky glucans that help it adhere to teeth.
qs.s: Medical Bacteriology and Entomology Exam 2020/2021 MCQs

qs.q: A 65-year-old woman complains of extreme dry mouth, difficulty swallowing, and recurrent dental caries. She is on multiple medications for hypertension and depression. What is the most common cause of her xerostomia?
o: Radiation therapy damage to bilateral parotid glands
Medications including anticholinergic and antidepressant agents
Sjögren syndrome with anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies
Bilateral parotid gland obstruction by sialolithiasis
qs.e: Medications are the most frequent cause of xerostomia, including anticholinergic, antidepressant, antihypertensive, and diuretic agents. Sjögren syndrome is the second most important cause.

ai.title: Dental Caries
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Dental caries is a biofilm‑driven, acid‑mediated demineralisation of tooth structure. In low‑resource settings it often co‑exists with malnutrition, HIV and poor oral hygiene, and can lead to pain, infection and systemic complications.

sections.p: Progressive loss of enamel and dentine caused by acid from bacterial fermentation of dietary carbohydrates. Diagnosis is clinical: visual inspection of cavitated lesions, probing with a dental explorer, and radiographs if available.
b: Visible cavitation or softened enamel
Explorer catches on rough surface
Radiolucency extending into dentine on bite‑wing X‑ray

sections.p: Use the International Caries Detection and Assessment System (ICDAS).
b: ICDAS 0 – sound tooth
ICDAS 1–2 – early enamel lesion (white spot)
ICDAS 3–4 – localized enamel breakdown
ICDAS 5–6 – extensive dentine involvement

sections.p: Caries results from the interaction of bacteria, diet, host factors and time.
b: Streptococcus mutans and Lactobacillus spp. (most common)
Frequent consumption of fermentable carbs, especially sugary drinks
Reduced salivary flow (e.g., due to dehydration, medications, Sjögren’s)
Poor oral hygiene and lack of fluoride
Co‑morbidities: HIV, malnutrition, chronic diarrhoea, use of herbal preparations that dry mouth

sections.p: Early lesions are asymptomatic. Progression leads to toothache, sensitivity, visible pits, and eventually abscess formation.
b: Sharp, intermittent pain triggered by hot/cold
Visible dark or brown pits on occlusal surfaces
Swelling of the gingiva or periapical area if pulp involved
Difficulty chewing, weight loss in children

t.b: Confirms presence, extent and activity of lesions; guides staging
Detects interproximal lesions not visible clinically; if unavailable, use trans‑illumination or tactile probing
Identifies hyposalivation contributing to rapid progression; if unavailable, assess xerostomia history
Confirms high mutans streptococci load; rarely needed in routine care

sections.p: Complications can become life‑threatening, especially in immunocompromised patients.
b: Acute dental abscess with facial swelling, trismus, fever – risk of cellulitis or sepsis
Pulp necrosis leading to periapical osteomyelitis
Severe pain causing inability to eat → malnutrition
Spread of infection to mediastinum in deep neck spaces

sections.p: Treat the active lesion, control infection, and modify risk factors.
b: Topical fluoride (2% NaF varnish) – remineralises early lesions
Silver diamine fluoride for arresting cavitated lesions when drilling not feasible
Restorative treatment (fillings) for ICDAS 3‑6 – use glass‑ionomer in low‑resource settings for fluoride release
Extraction of non‑restorable teeth, especially if causing abscess
Analgesia with paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment
Antibiotics (amoxicillin) only for spreading infection or systemic signs

sections.p: Regular review and community‑level prevention are essential.
b: Recall every 6 months for visual exam and fluoride application
Oral hygiene education – twice‑daily brushing with fluoride toothpaste
Dietary counselling – limit sugary snacks and drinks
Fluoridated water or salt where feasible
Screen for xerostomia and treat underlying causes

sections.p: Conditions that mimic caries on visual exam.
b: Dental erosion (acid from reflux or diet, no bacterial plaque)
Developmental enamel hypoplasia (congenital pits, not bacterial)
Traumatic tooth fracture (sharp edge, not decay)
Radiographs may miss early lesions if exposure is poor – rely on clinical signs
Salivary flow test can be normal in early xerostomia – use symptom history
White‑spot lesions may be mistaken for fluorosis; assess diet and plaque

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid facial swelling, difficulty breathing, or trismus

faq.a: Yes, when the infection spreads to the pulp or periapical tissues, it can trigger a systemic febrile response.

faq.q: Is fluoride safe for children under five?
faq.a: Topical fluoride varnish is safe and recommended; avoid swallowing large amounts of toothpaste.

faq.q: Why choose silver diamine fluoride over a filling?
faq.a: It arrests decay without drilling, useful when equipment or patient cooperation is limited, though it stains the lesion black.

exam: A 7‑year‑old presents with a brown pit on a molar and intermittent pain – what is the next step in management? — Assess lesion depth clinically; if ICDAS 3‑4, place a glass‑ionomer restoration; if only early enamel, apply fluoride varnish.

A patient with HIV reports frequent mouth sores and new carious lesions – which systemic factor is most likely contributing? — Hyposalivation from antiretroviral therapy and immune suppression increase bacterial load.
You cannot obtain a bite‑wing X‑ray; how do you stage the caries? — Use ICDAS visual criteria and tactile probing; treat based on clinical stage.
What distinguishes dental erosion from caries on examination? — Erosion shows smooth, glazed surfaces without plaque; caries has rough, plaque‑laden cavitation.

A child with severe caries refuses to eat and has lost weight – what complication should you anticipate? — Malnutrition and possible growth delay; assess nutritional status and consider supplemental feeding.

Why is amoxicillin preferred over clindamycin for a dental abscess in a malaria‑endemic area? — Amoxicillin covers common oral streptococci and has a lower risk of inducing Clostridioides difficile, which is already prevalent in low‑resource settings.

During a community screening you find many early white‑spot lesions but no fluoride toothpaste is available – what is the best interim preventive measure? — Educate on reducing sugary snack frequency and encourage rinsing with water after meals.
A patient presents with a blackened lesion after silver diamine fluoride application – does this indicate treatment failure? — No; black staining is expected and indicates arrested decay.
